title.narrative: Implementation rate of DIOS audit and evaluation recommendations

description.narrative: Implementation rate of DIOS audit and evaluation recommendations

comment.narrative: UNRWA Annual Operational Report AOR 2021 DIOS issues audit and evaluation recommendations to management at which point a timebound action plan is developed and agreed in support of their implementation. The length of time required to implement a recommendation depends on the complexity of the issues being addressed and the resources required to act. DIOS regularly follows up on the timely implementation of recommendations with recommendation owners and requests formal implementation status updates on a biannual basis.During the reporting period 72.2 per cent of recommendations 78 out of 108 stemming from audits and evaluations issued in 2018 and 2019 were implemented within a twoyear period. The result fell slightly short of the 80 per cent target due to the low implementation rate in 2019 and 2020 caused by the impact of Agency austerity measures and operational disruption caused by COVID19 from March 2020. These factors most influenced the implementation rate for recommendations stemming from 2018 evaluation and audit assignments. UNRWAs performance in implementing audit recommendations issued in 2019 was almost to 90 per cent however the average rate informing the indicator was negatively impacted by the low implementation rate of 59 per cent for recommendations issued in 2018 influenced by the aforementioned factors. Staff turnover in key positions also impacted the implementation rate.The average combined implementation rate for central and decentralized evaluation recommendations for 2018 and 2019 was 71 per cent. Similar to the trend for audit the implementation of recommendations issued in 2018 at 64 per cent was lower than the rate achieved for recommendations stemming from 2019 evaluations which reached 85 per cent.As referenced above DIOS reports results on the implementation rate of audit and evaluation recommendations within a twoyear timeframe. In the upcoming Strategic Plan 202328 this indicator will be adjusted to measure Agency performance in implementing recommendations against an agreed i.e. not automatically set at two years implementation timeline. This change will facilitate a more accurate assessment of performance with due consideration extended to the time and financial resources required to implement a recommendation.

title.narrative: Percentage of UNRWA installations receiving two or more neutrality inspections annually

description.narrative: Percentage of UNRWA installations receiving two or more neutrality inspections annually

comment.narrative: One of the ways that UNRWA safeguards humanitarian principles is through regular inspections of its installations. To this end UNRWA conducted 1794 inspections of 988 installations during the reporting period 53 per cent more than in 2020 when 1171 inspections were conducted. The Agency endeavoured to ensure that as many installations as possible were inspected and by the end of the year all installations had been inspected once170 and 83 per cent of installations were inspected twice.Despite enhanced performance in comparison to 2020 UNRWA underachieved against the 2021 target due to both Agencywide and fieldspecific challenges. In this regard i movement restrictions and staff shortages related to COVID19 continued to hamper inspections in all fields particularly during the first half of 2021 ii in the West Bank general strikes called by Palestinian factions in February and May impacted on the inspection rate during the first half of the year iii in Lebanon the fuel crisis and continuing civil unrest limited the number of installations that could be visited and iv in Gaza inspections were impacted by heightened political tensions in relation to the planned PA elections and the May hostilities. As a result inspections were temporarily suspended.Inspections conducted during the reporting period identified 1142 neutrality issues 474 of which were reported for the first time. Of these issues 76 per cent pertained to installation maintenance e.g. issues relating to no weapons signs UN flags and UN signboards with anecdotal evidence pointing to the lack of funds being behind the inability to resolve these issues. Data shows that 40 per cent of these maintenance issues are persistent compared to just 25 per cent of nonmaintenance related issues.

title.narrative: UNRWAs performance on the UNSWAP framework of indicators

description.narrative: UNRWAs performance on the UNSWAP framework of indicators

comment.narrative: UNRWA Annual Operational Report AOR 2021 Pg. 26During the reporting period UNRWA enhanced its performance against the UN Systemwide Action Plan on Gender Equality and the Empowerment of Women UNSWAP 2.0 indicators. In this regard the Agency met or exceeded the requirements for 11 of the 17 performance indicators an increase of one indicator over the previous year. Progress was made despite the absence of additional resources and against a backdrop of continued operational disruption caused by COVID19 and UNRWAs ongoing financial crisis. Performance against UNSWAP 2.0 performance indicator 4 on evaluation improved from approaching to meeting requirements by virtue of aligning Agency evaluation practices with the United Nations Evaluation Groups UNEG Guidance on Integrating Human Rights and Gender Equality in Evaluation. In their assessment of UNRWAs performance against UNSWAP 2.0 indicators UN Women encouraged the Agency to prioritize the implementation of performance indicator 10 on financial resource allocation the only indicator still classified as missing requirements and four indicators assessed as approaching requirements.

title.narrative: Average daily medical consultations per doctor

description.narrative: Average daily medical consultations per doctor

comment.narrative: Throughout the MTS strategic period UNRWA has attempted to reduce the average number of daily medical consultations per doctor to meet the Agency ide2022 target of 72.4. Despite progress prior to the onset of COVID19 this target has been difficult to achieve due to the chronic funding crisis that has limited the recruitment of additional medical staff. The pandemic led to exaggerated performance gains in 2020 due to a steep decline in the number of inperson Primary Health Clinic PHC consultations at Agency health centres. In 2021 the number of patient consultations partially rebounded due to the introduction of COVID19 vaccines the resumption of nonessential health services in the second half of the year enhanced compliance with COVID19 preventativeprotective measures and improved understanding of the nature of the disease. During the reporting period UNRWA provided 6156188 inperson consultations 3767928 female2388260 male some 357284 more than in 2020 anda further 844518 telemedicine consultations across Gaza 767904 Jordan 28211 Syria 46379 and the West Bank 2024. Children under five accounted for 379431 inperson consultations an increase of 29630 from the previous year. A similar trend was observed for MHPSS consultations which increased to 76477 in 2021 from 50810 in 2020. Reflecting this increase in patient consultations the average daily medical consultations per Agency doctor increased to 66.3 from 58.8 in 2020 while the average consultation time per doctor was reduced to just under three minutes from just over three minutes the previous year. UNRWAs norms for doctors target an average consultation time of five minutes. Unfortunately as referenced above ongoing financial constraints do not allow for the recruitment of a sufficient number of medical officers to achieve this target.

title.narrative: Percentage of protection mainstreaming recommendations from internal protection audits implemented

description.narrative: Percentage of protection mainstreaming recommendations from internal protection audits implemented

comment.narrative: The most recent round of protection audits was finalized in July 2019 and resulted in 104 recommendations including measures to ensure i nondiscriminatory and meaningful access to UNRWA services ii the safety and dignity of Palestine refugees iii accountability to affected populations AAP and iv Palestine refugee participation and empowerment. During the reporting period the implementation of protection audit recommendations was hampered by funding shortages the turnover of key staff and continued disruption of operations as a result of COVID19 which necessitated thepostponement of some planned activities. Despite this by the end of 2021 63 recommendations had been fully implemented including in relation to the a establishment of systems for the identification and referral of students at risk of dropout or longterm absenteeism b implementation of a tool to assess and mitigate protection risks associated with shelter rehabilitation c establishment of appointment and queuing systems at all Agency health facilities to ensure better access reduce waiting times for disabled elderly and other vulnerable patients and d introduction of postdistribution monitoring PDM for unaccompanied and separated children who receive cash support to address protection risks.A further 41 recommendations remained under implementation and are anticipated to either be finalized in 2022 or carried over into the next round of protection audits. Recommendations that are anticipated to be completed in 2022 include the i assessment of peer mediation in reducing violence in schools ii streamlined approval process for emergency shelter rehabilitation cases and iii implementation of a protectionfocused satisfaction survey for patients at UNRWA health centres.In 2021 a Department of Internal Oversight Services DIOSled evaluation of the protection audit mechanism confirmed its effectiveness in identifying and addressing protection mainstreaming challenges in Agency service delivery.105 The evaluation also identified the need for i the planning phase of protection audits to be strengthened through the identification and analysis of learning from previous audit cycles ii a more systematic and standardized approach to the formulation and approval of protection audit recommendations and iii enhanced tracking of and followup on the implementation of audit recommendations. Evaluation conclusions and recommendations have been incorporated into a revised methodology that will form the basis for the next cycle of protection audits that will begin in 2022.

During the reporting period the implementation of protection audit recommendations was hampered by funding shortages the turnover of key staff and continued disruption of operations as a result of COVID19 which necessitated thepostponement of some planned activities. Despite this by the end of 2021 63 recommendations had been fully implemented including in relation to the a establishment of systems for the identification and referral of students at risk of dropout or longterm absenteeism b implementation of a tool to assess and mitigate protection risks associated with shelter rehabilitation c establishment of appointment and queuing systems at all Agency health facilities to ensure better access reduce waiting times for disabled elderly and other vulnerable patients and d introduction of postdistribution monitoring PDM for unaccompanied and separated children who receive cash support to address protection risks.A further 41 recommendations remained under implementation and are anticipated to either be finalized in 2022 or carried over into the next round of protection audits. Recommendations that are anticipated to be completed in 2022 include the i assessment of peer mediation in reducing violence in schools ii streamlined approval process for emergency shelter rehabilitation cases and iii implementation of a protectionfocused satisfaction survey for patients at UNRWA health centres.In 2021 a Department of Internal Oversight Services DIOSled evaluation of the protection audit mechanism confirmed its effectiveness in identifying and addressing protection mainstreaming challenges in Agency service delivery.105 The evaluation also identified the need for i the planning phase of protection audits to be strengthened through the identification and analysis of learning from previous audit cycles ii a more systematic and standardized approach to the formulation and approval of protection audit recommendations and iii enhanced tracking of and followup on the implementation of audit recommendations. Evaluation conclusions and recommendations have been incorporated into a revised methodology that will form the basis for the next cycle of protection audits that will begin in 2022.

title.narrative: Stability in the number of UNRWA schools/educational facilities providing services to Palestine refugees

description.narrative: The number of schools is dependent on several factors, including whether enrolment of students is increasing or decreasing in each locality, the merger of smaller schools into larger ones, the availability of funding and land for the construction of new schools and future decisions on the reconstruction of damaged schools in Syria; however is expected to remain relatively stable given that more than half a million children attend UNRWA schools on a dailybasis.

comment.narrative: For a second successive year the education of Palestine refugee children was disrupted by COVID19. In line with host government decisions students enrolled in UNRWA schools were taught through a combination of inperson remote and blended lessons as schools continued to face intermittent closures or in the case of Gaza and Syria the academic year was curtailed in response to the evolving epidemiological situation. Despite these challenges the Agency succeeded in maintaining the learning process for 539770 students 267636 girls 272134 boys enrolled in 710 schools in line with SDG 4. The majority of results against UNRWA performance indicators for the 202021 academic year were assessed as ahead of plan. The Agency constructed reconstructed or upgraded four schools to meet UNRWA education reform protection and safety requirements.
